Title: A lightweight LSTM-based open- set RF fingerprinting identification for edge deployment
Text:
A lightweight LSTM-based open-
set RF fingerprinting identification 
for edge deployment
Yuxuan Hu1, Yutong Fu2 & Ye Chen3
With the rapid advancement of deep learning techniques, numerous neural networks have been 
successfully developed for radio frequency (RF) fingerprinting identification. In this work, we propose 
a lightweight yet reliable neural network framework featuring a 9-layer architecture based on the long 
short-term memory (LSTM) strategy, designed for efficient open-set fingerprinting identification. The 
simulated beacon frames model real-world propagation effects by incorporating random modulation, 
power amplifier nonlinearity, multi-path fading, inherent radio noise, and additive channel noise. We 
extensively evaluate the identification accuracy and efficiency of our LSTM network identification 
against well-known deep learning models such as ResNet (144 layers) and GoogleNet (177 layers). 
The evaluation covers a wide range of parameters, including transmitter variability (s), number of 
transmitters (N), frames per transmitter (F P T ) and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Our results show 
that the LSTM network maintains an accuracy of more than 96% in SNR ≥20 with F P T = 200, 
even with up to N = 1000 transmitters. At lower values (F P T ≤100, 6 ≤SNR ≤15 dB), our 
LSTM network outperforms GoogleNet and matches ResNet in accuracy. Furthermore, it achieves a 
training acceleration of up to 116.7× for N = 100 and F P T = 200, with inference times under 2 
seconds. Meanwhile here, the usage of VRAM is reduced by up to 22.4×, and the model disk size is 
under 1 MB. Experiments on devices, including a high performance computing (HPC) node, a personal 
computer (PC), and three smartphones, demonstrate that the optimal strategy depends on the scale of 
the problem: local processing for N = 12, remote training with local inference for N = 100, and full 
remote processing for N = 1000.
With the advent of the Internet of Things (IoT), the dramatic proliferation of wireless devices, such as cell 
phones, wireless audio and video transmitters, motion detectors, WLAN, vehicles and aircrafts, has brought 
great convenience to users around the world1,2. However, due to the broadcast nature of wireless transmissions, 
many radio frequency (RF) devices today are unsecured and therefore vulnerable to malicious attacks and false 
impersonations1,3. For example, long-term evolution (LTE) systems have been reported to have been exposed 
to physical threats including RF jamming, spoofing, and sniffing due to the loophole of the protocol standard 
defined by 3GPP4,5. Wi-Fi handshakes are vulnerable to key reinstallation attacks, which exploit design or 
implementation flaws in cryptographic protocols to force the reuse of an already-in-use key6. Security remains 
one of the primary challenges in emerging 5G-IoT architectures, as end-user data must be authenticated and 
safeguarded against eavesdropping and interference7.
To mitigate potential attacks and impersonations, significant research efforts have been dedicated to developing 
reliable identification schemes that enhance the security of RF devices. Leveraging the inherent variability 
in transmitter front-ends caused by manufacturing processes, RF fingerprinting technology has garnered 
considerable attention as an additional security layer, complementing encryption for wireless devices8–12. These 
unique variations, such as IQ imbalance, DC offset, oscillator imperfections, mixer imbalance, and non-linear 
power amplifier gain, alter the operating point of the transmitted signal within the in-phase/quadrature (IQ) 
representation space13–16. Traditional RF fingerprinting schemes are primarily based on the waveform of the 
received transmitter signal for effective feature acquisition and device classification12. As an example, Nguyen 
et al. proposed a nonparametric Bayesian method for detecting the number of devices and classifying multiple 
devices in an unsupervised and passive manner17. However, traditional RF fingerprinting often requires expert 
knowledge, making it difficult to scale and generalize for large-scale IoT systems18,19.

Fortunately, this limitation of traditional RF fingerprinting schemes has been largely overcome with the 
collaboration of artificial intelligence in recent years. Many machine learning and deep learning algorithms have 
successfully learned from a large dataset of signals collected from the transmitter and have outperformed today’s 
expertly-engineered RF systems1,16,20. Merchant et al. developed a framework for training a convolutional neural 
network (CNN) using the complex time domain baseband error signal and demonstrated 92.29% identification 
accuracy in a set of seven 2.4 GHz commercial ZigBee devices, and its robustness is demonstrated for the 
SNR range between 10 and 40 dB21. Baldini et al. conducted a comparative experiment using different CNN 
architectures and evaluated their performance for a wide SNR range between −3 and 57 dB for 12 wireless 
devices with and without additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN)22. With access to powerful GPUs, larger neural 
networks have also been trained using waveform data collected from up to 10,000 devices23–25. Such large neural 
networks for RF fingerprinting typically operate on a remote central server, which necessitates the transfer of a 
large volume of data for training and inference. For example, a 7  TB experimental dataset and a 400 GB dataset 
provided by DARPA, which includes hundreds of thousands of transmissions from thousands of WiFi and 
ADS-B devices under varying SNR conditions, have been used to fully assess the impact of the wireless channel 
on CNN-based fingerprinting algorithms26. Moreover, in addition to the known device classification27–29, 
specific attention has also been paid to open-set device recognition to reject unknown malicious devices that 
gain access to the network2,30–32.
To overcome the power and memory constraints of edge devices, edge computing has been proposed for 
efficient RF fingerprint identification. This decentralized approach involves training a deep neural network in 
a central cloud before deploying it to a low-power edge device for local inference16. However, it may become 
extremely insecure to transmit and store RF features on the public network for certain security-sensitive edge 
devices. To avoid this, a distributed machine learning method with optimized communication cost is proposed. 
Their training takes more than 2000 seconds with an accuracy greater than 94% for a total number of 100,000 
signals from 20 devices31. Recently, a federated transfer learning mechanism has also been designed without 
compromising data privacy through a collaborative neural network33. Although the security risk associated with 
data transfer is mitigated, the deployment of neural networks in varying device configurations can compromise 
their universality. In addition, techniques such as pruning have been used to develop compressed neural 
networks, addressing significant computational costs and accelerating the training process18,34,35. For example, a 
compression factor of 27.2 for convolutional layers is achieved while incurring a negligible decrease in prediction 
accuracy of less than 1 percent16. An earlier LSTM neural network has already been proposed. However, it is 
only used for the automatic identification of hardware-specific features and identical transmitters in the presence 
of strong noise36. The design of a lightweight neural network and the subsequent comprehensive study on its 
RF identification (RFID) performance that incorporates the effects of device variability, device number, frame 
number per device, and SNR, as well as its deployment strategy to today are still far from a satisfactory level.
In this study, we propose a lightweight yet reliable neural network with a 9-layer architecture based on the 
LSTM strategy for efficient open-set RFID. Such RFID systems, which employ a deployment strategy based 
on systematic evaluation, are particularly valuable for resource-constrained edge environments within the IoT 
ecosystem, but they remain less explored to date12,16,20,37–43. To achieve this, we employ a previous experiment-
based power amplifier nonlinearity model to construct realistic transmitter models. We then generate beacon 
frames incorporating multi-path fading, radio impairments, and AWGN in a parallel manner using multiple 
CPU cores for acceleration. This enables us to evaluate the RFID performance efficiently using up to 1000 
transmitters and 800 frames per transmitter. The identification performance of our LSTM-based neural network 
is extensively evaluated in a wide parameter space by comparing it with two well-known deep neural networks, 
ResNet and GoogleNet. Finally, we test our LSTM-based neural network on multiple edge devices, including one 
HPC node, one PC, and three smartphones, using CPU and GPU processors for processing.
Methodology
Data generation and pre-processing
We use MATLAB (version: matlabR2023b, URL: mathworks.com/products/matlab.html) WLAN Toolbox 
to generate the RF beacon frames, as shown in Fig. 1a. Each complex baseband signal x(t) includes both in-
phase and quadrature components, and adheres to the 802.11a/g/n/ac non-HT packet format. To account 
for transmitter-specific power amplifier nonlinearity, we employ Saleh’s model to obtain the RF output signal 
f(x(t))44. This model relates the input amplitude r to the output amplitude A(r) via A(r) = αr/(1 + βr2)
44. The two model parameters, α and β, are statistically determined from the experimental measurement of 
101 curves from the 7 transmitters. As shown in Fig. 1b, α is first determined using the experimentally fitted 
normal distribution of the transmitter group of variability s, α = αmax −∆α(1 −e−x/s). Like the setup in 
previous work45, we choose αmax = 3.0 and ∆α = 1.8 to represent a normal distribution of N(1.5, s), and x 
is a uniformly distributed random number between 0 and 1. β is then obtained using the linear regression line 
fitted from the experiment β = −1.1 + 0.2α. In general, a large value of s corresponds to low-cost devices with 
high variability.
After that, a system object of rfFingerprintingNonHTFrontEnd is created in the MATLAB WLAN toolbox 
to detect and receive the output RF signal f(x(t)). To mimic the real-world environment, we employ the system 
object of comm.RayleighChannel to include the multi-path fading effect due to signal reflection and scattering. 
In this work, we use a sample rate of 20 MHz and zero maximum Doppler shift for the multi-path channel. Then, 
channel impairments including phase noise, frequency offset, and DC offset are also introduced to obtain the 
RF signal h(f(x(t))). Finally, AWGN with a specific SNR denoted as n(t) is added to the signal waveform and 
the received signal is represented by y(t) = h(f(x(t))) + n(t). Only the L-LTF segment with a fixed length of 
80 µs× 20MHz = 160 (for both the in-phase and quadrature components in our present frequency domain 
representation, respectively), which belongs to the preamble part of the generated RF signal y(t), will be fed into

fingerprinting tasks.
LSTM-based neural network
As shown in Fig. 1c, we propose a lightweight neural network based on the LSTM strategy for the identification 
of open-set RF fingerprints. The 9-layer architecture of our LSTM-based neural network consists of one flatten 
layer, two pairs of LSTM and dropout layers, one fully connected layer, one softmax layer and a classification 
layer. The flatten layer is used to reshape the two-dimensional in-phase and quadrature input data into a single 
dimension before being processed through the two LSTM layers. Two dropout layers with both probability 
0.5 are introduced to enhance the model generalization and avoid data overfitting. The output of the second 
LSTM layer is fed into a fully connected layer, which maps the extracted features to multiple output categories. 
The fully connected layer outputs are then passed through a softmax layer, which converts these outputs into a 
probabilistic distribution. This transformation facilitates multi-class classification by providing probability scores 
for each category. The final classification decision is made based on these probabilities. This architecture ensures 
that the model can effectively learn and classify RF fingerprints while maintaining computational efficiency and 
robust generalization.
The L-LTF segments generated are first randomly shuffled and then divided into three sets: training (80%), 
validation (10%), and test (10%). The training process employs the following key parameters: a maximum of 
20 epochs, an initial learning rate of 0.008, a learning rate drop factor of 0.5, and a L2 regularization of 0.001. 
Furthermore, the training data are randomly shuffled at each epoch to enhance mixing and prevent overfitting. 
For a fair evaluation of RFID performance, we compared accuracy, training, and inference time consumption, 
as well as the use of VRAM and disk storage of our LSTM-based neural network, with those of ResNet and 
GoogleNet. In our study, the term “accuracy” refers specifically to the accuracy of Top-1 classification, the 
proportion of test instances for which the system’s device identity predicted above matches the true transmitter

Results and discussions
The neural network’s open-set RF identification performance, including identification accuracy, training/
inference time, VRAM, and storage usage, is critical for its successful deployment on edge devices. This work also 
compares the performance of our LSTM-based network with that of ResNet, GoogleNet, and other previously 
proposed lightweight architectures. All results are averaged from the 100 independent trials.
Transmitter variability
We first investigate the impact of transmitter variability on the open-set RF identification performance of our 
LSTM-based neural network by considering s = 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0. At the same time, a fixed 
number of transmitters of N = 100 is chosen, while the frame number per transmitter FPT ∈[50, 200] with 
a step of 50 and SNR ∈[10, 40] with a step of 5 are used. As shown in Fig. 2a, for larger FPT = 200, all 
three neural networks can achieve an identification accuracy greater than 90% for tested transmitter variability 
s ∈[0, 1] and SNR ∈[10, 40]. Meanwhile, the adverse impact of smaller variability s on identification accuracy 
is evident. For example, the identification accuracy is 97.5% at s = 0.005 in our LSTM-based neural network, 
while it increases to 99.2% at s = 1.0. This trend was also reported in a previous study45. In addition, we can 
see that the identification accuracy from our LSTM-based neural network is overall steadier than the other two 
neural networks, especially the ResNet.
When FPT is reduced to 50, an identification accuracy greater than 90% is maintained only at larger 
SNR = 20, 30, and 40, as shown in Fig.  2b. For SNR = 20, the identification accuracy of our LSTM-
based neural network is close to that of GoogleNet and slightly lower than that of ResNet. For example, 
when s = 0.5, the identification accuracies are 96.2% and 96.4% for the neural network based on LSTM 
and GoogleNet, respectively, while it becomes slightly higher for ResNet of 99.7%. At a smaller SNR = 10, 
the reduction in identification accuracy is clear. The accuracy of our LSTM-based neural network is between 
GoogleNet and ResNet. For example, when s = 0.5, the identification accuracy is 65.4%, 88.1%, and 98.4% 
for GoogleNet, LSTM-based neural network and ResNet, respectively. Overall, SNR has a greater impact on 
identification accuracy than transmitter variability (s), particularly for a small number of frames per transmitter 
(FPT=50).
For a comprehensive comparison, we also recorded the training time, VRAM, and storage usage of these 
three different neural networks. Due to their deep-layer architecture (177 layers for ResNet and 144 layers 
for GoogleNet), the average training times for both ResNet and GoogleNet are 1936.5 s and 948.3 s under 
FPT = 200, and 339.0 s and 181.2 s under FPT = 50, respectively. However, the corresponding training 
time for our neural network with a comparatively shallower 9-layer architecture based on the LSTM strategy 
is significantly reduced to 16.6 s and 9.6 s, which represents a speedup of up to 116.7, as shown in Fig. 2c. 
During training, ResNet and GoogleNet take a VRAM of 7.6 GB and 4.4 GB for FPT = 50; it increases further 
to 11.4  GB and 10.6  GB as FPT increases to 200. In contrast, our LSTM-based neural network only uses 
0.51 GB for both FPT = 50 and 200, which produces a VRAM reduction factor of up to 22.4. After training 
the neural network, ResNet and GoogleNet take a disk storage of 91.0 MB and 25.3 MB, respectively, while 
only 0.9 MB is used for our LSTM-based neural network. This storage size of 0.9 MB from our LSTM-based 
neural network is also lower than the 2.41 MB required by the lightweight SE-MobileNet43, owing to the reduced 
parameter count of our model (0.12 M vs. ≈0.58 M)37,43. Our LSTM-based neural network demonstrates both 
high identification accuracy and notable reductions in training time and VRAM/disk usage. It is particularly

High SNR and low SNR
Next, we conduct an extensive open-set RF identification study. We vary the number of transmitters, N, from 
100 to 1000 in increments of 100, and consider five frames-per-transmitter (FPT) values: 50, 100, 200, 400, 
and 800. The transmitter variability is held constant at s = 0.5. We first focus on the high SNR regime with 
SNR ∈[15, 60] and the identification accuracy results for FPT = 50, 100, 200, 400, and 800 are shown in 
Fig. 3a–e. We can see that the identification accuracy overall increases with higher SNR for a given FPT. For 
example, with N = 1000 and FPT = 200, the identification accuracy improves from 86.7% to 99.2% to 
99.6% as SNR increases from 15 to 30 to 60 dB, respectively (Fig. 3c). However, the overall accuracy of the 
identification decreases as the transmitter number N increases. For example, at SNR = 15 dB and FPT = 400, 
the identification accuracy decreases from 98.4% to 96.7% and finally to 90.9% as the number of transmitters 
(N) increases from 100 to 500 to 1000 (Fig. 3d). In addition, when both SNR and the transmitter number N are 
constant, increasing the frame number per transmitter (FPT) leads to higher identification accuracy.
We continue to examine the open-set RF identification performance of our LSTM-based neural network in 
the low SNR range of SNR ∈[6, 14] with a step of 1, where FPT is uniformly set between [50, 400] with 
a step of 50. Generating RF beacon frames in this low SNR range is challenging, so we limit the number of 
transmitters to N=12 (including 8 known devices and 4 unknown devices). The results of the identification 
accuracy are presented in Fig. 3f. We can see that, compared to the high SNR range scenario discussed above, an 
identification accuracy greater than 90% can still be achieved with our LSTM-based neural network. However, 
an evident drop in identification accuracy can be observed for small FPT = 50. For example, under SNR = 6 
and FPT = 50, the identification accuracy is 53.3%, which is still higher than the lightweight SE-MobileNet 
at higher SNR (e.g., SNR = 15) proposed in43. As SNR gradually increases from 6 to 14, the identification 
accuracy improves to 90.0%. In Fig. 4, we also present the confusion matrices obtained from one trial within 
the low SNR range with N = 12 and s = 0.5. Again, we can see that the identification accuracy is relatively 
low, at 53.5% for SNR = 6 and FPT = 50. However, when either SNR or FPT increases, the identification 
accuracy increases markedly to 95.0% and 97.5% for (SNR, FPT) = (14, 50) and (6, 200), respectively.
Deployment experiments on edge devices and performance
Note that our LSTM-based neural network is trained on simulated signals representing up to 1000 devices, not 
on data physically collected from that number of actual edge devices. To validate the applicability of our LSTM-
based neural network on real-world edge devices, we have also tested its identification performance on a variety 
of devices using MATLAB or TensorFlow (version: Tensorflow v2.10, URL: tensorflow.org/install). As shown 
in Fig. 5a, these devices include one HPC node at the South China University of Technology (use 1 NVIDIA 
A800 GPU or 64 Intel Xeon6458 CPU cores), one PC (use 1 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 GPU or 14 Intel Core 
i5-13600KF CPU cores), and three smartphones (use Kirin 970, Kirin 980 and Snapdragon 8 Gen3 smartphone 
processors, respectively). In the experiment, we first set s = 0.5, N = 12, FPT = 200, and SNR = 20. The 
training time and inference time on different devices are presented in Fig. 5b,c, respectively. We can see that 
most training processes on HPC node and PC using CPU and GPU can be finished in less than 5 seconds, 
while it may take a slightly longer time of 27.9 s with TensorFlow using 64 Xeon6458 CPU cores on the HPC 
node. In contrast, the training times on smartphones are much longer, and they are 210.7, 471.9 and 359.5 s for

Finally, we present an ablation study of our LSTM-based RFID framework on PC under various parameter 
combinations of (N, SNR, FPT), as summarized in Table 2. The full LSTM-based model achieves high accuracy, 
often exceeding 98% and mostly above 95%, across most scenarios, particularly under high SNR conditions and 
with more frames (FPT = 200). As expected, performance deteriorates consistently across all model variants 
under low SNR (10 dB) compared to high SNR (20 dB), especially with larger numbers of devices (N = 100 or 
1000), where accuracy can drop into the 80% range. In several trials (e.g., 1, 4, 10, 11, 12), removing either LSTM 
layer results in a noticeable decline in accuracy, confirming that both layers contribute meaningfully to optimal 
performance. However, in certain high-SNR, high-FPT scenarios (e.g., Trials 3, 5, 6, 9), the difference between 
the full and ablated models becomes negligible ( 0.1–0.3%), indicating strong model robustness under ideal 
conditions. No consistent trend emerges suggesting that one LSTM layer is substantially more critical than the 
other; rather, their importance appears context-dependent. For a fixed number of devices and SNR, increasing 
FPT almost universally improves accuracy across all model configurations, underscoring the importance of 
sufficient data samples per device for reliable identification. In contrast, for fixed SNR and FPT, increasing 
the number of devices generally reduces accuracy due to the increased classification complexity. Nonetheless,

Conclusions
In this work, we propose a lightweight yet reliable 9-layer neural network based on the LSTM strategy for 
efficient open-set RF fingerprinting identification. The simulated beacon frames used for training incorporate 
random modulation, power amplifier nonlinearity, multi-path fading, radio impairments, and additive noise. 
The accuracy and efficiency of our LSTM-based neural network are extensively evaluated across a wide 
parameter space and compared with the well-known ResNet and GoogleNet architectures. An identification 
accuracy greater than 96% is consistently obtained for FPT ≥200 and SNR ≥20. For lower FPT ≤100 
and 6 ≤SNR ≤15, the LSTM-based neural network still outperforms GoogleNet and behaves close to ResNet. 
In particular, a significant speed-up of up to 116.7 is achieved in training when N = 100 and FPT = 200, and 
the inference time falls below 2 s. Meanwhile, the usage of VRAM is also reduced by a factor of up to 22.4, and 
the disk storage of the trained neural network based on LSTM is less than 1 MB. Our experiments reveal that the 
options of local training and inference, remote training and local inference, and remote training and inference 
become more suitable for N = 12, 100, and 1000, respectively. The subsequent ablation study confirms that 
both LSTM layers are critical for the model’s performance. These findings demonstrate that a lightweight LSTM-
based neural network can achieve high accuracy in open-set RF fingerprinting while significantly reducing 
computational cost, training time, and storage requirements, allowing practical and energy-efficient deployment 
in edge devices.
Limitations and future work
The current work relies on simulated data that, while incorporating realistic impairments, may not encompass 
the full complexity of real-world RF environments. In addition, the evaluation is limited to 1000 devices; 
scalability to larger IoT networks remains unverified. Future work should validate the model using large-scale 
and real-world signal captures under diverse channel conditions. Meanwhile, hybrid architectures and further 
network compression could also be explored to reduce energy and latency for ultra-low-power devices.
